# Was Airbyte Cloud hacked in the Nov 2026 security incident?

**Confirmed.** Yes, by Airbyte's own account: it says an attacker had access to its systems before it blocked them. How they got in, who they are and what they reached are not established.

Incident: Airbyte Cloud security incident, Nov 2026. Also reported as the Airbyte Cloud outage and the Airbyte cyberattack. First published Nov 21, 2026; last updated Nov 21, 2026, 4:35 PM ET.

> **Not verified: initial investigation only.** Nothing on this page is absolutely confirmed. It is an early look based only on publicly available sources, and it should not be treated as verified fact. Even items labeled "Confirmed" only mean a public source reports them. Made for entertainment using AI. Not endorsed by Airbyte, Salesforce, any government agency, news outlet, company, or anyone else named.

This is the current answer, not a final verdict.

## The latest

Nov 21, 2026, 4:35 PM ET: **Airbyte's X posts now linked directly; no new facts.** No new Airbyte status update since 1:00 AM ET Nov 21, no incident report, no change to Salesforce advisory 20000278, no new Tier 1/2 source. Per editor note, Airbyte's X statement (Nov 17) and 'back online' post (Nov 20) are now cited directly from x.com (s008, s009) instead of the third-party mirror (s003, kept for the record). The Nov 20 'back online' time is now 2:54 AM ET from the post itself. No label changes. Privacy check done.

## At a glance

- Status: monitoring
- Size: Regional. Airbyte Cloud moves data between many companies' apps and databases, and every customer lost service for days. Airbyte says fewer than 1% of customers were directly affected. Salesforce also cut access. The full count is unknown.
- Who is affected: Companies that use Airbyte Cloud to sync data. API connectors for Salesforce, HubSpot, Zendesk and others were still down as of 1:00 AM ET Nov 21. Affected customers were contacted by Airbyte; others need only watch its status page.

| Value | What | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| <1% | Customers affected, per Airbyte | Airbyte's own figure; not checked by anyone else |
| 15 | API connectors still down | As of 1:00 AM ET Nov 21, per Airbyte |
| 4:09 PM | Security incident announced (ET) | Nov 17, on Airbyte's status page |
| 4:33 PM | Salesforce advisory (ET) | Nov 20; disabled the Airbyte app |

### Known so far

- Airbyte says a security incident gave an attacker access to its systems; it blocked them and took Cloud offline on Nov 17.
- Airbyte Cloud was offline for days; the service began coming back on Nov 19.
- Airbyte says fewer than 1% of its customers were affected and that it contacted them.
- As of 1:00 AM ET Nov 21, 15 API connectors, Connector Builder and MCP were still down as a cautionary measure.
- Salesforce disabled the Airbyte connected app on Nov 20 and says this was not a Salesforce platform problem.

### Not known yet

- Whether customer data, credentials or metadata were accessed or taken.
- How the attacker got in. Airbyte says a full incident report is coming.
- Who is behind it, and what 'broader, global cyberattack' Airbyte means.
- Whether Salesforce or other platforms' customer data was reached through Airbyte.
- When the remaining 15 API connectors, Builder and MCP will return.
- Whether self-managed Airbyte installs were affected.

## What we checked and did not find

We looked for these and did not find them as of the latest check (2026-11-21T16:16:05-05:00).

- An Airbyte incident report or post-mortem with the cause. Airbyte's X account says one is coming once its security team finalizes it.
- Any statement on whether customer data, credentials or metadata were accessed or taken.
- Any government or independent analysis naming the attacker, or any claim of responsibility or ransom demand reported by press. We did not visit leak sites or trackers.
- A statement from HubSpot, Zendesk, Atlassian or other platforms about why their Airbyte connectors are down.
- Any Salesforce finding of unauthorized access to customer data. Its advisory says it will notify customers if it finds any.
- Coverage from a Tier 2 news outlet. Every outside article we found is a small security tracker or blog, and they repeat Airbyte's statements.
- A source that ties this incident to any other company's breach or to a named campaign.
